"He's very old ... he's been through many, many things. This was his 66th movie, or something like that." Sagnier describes her character, Gabrielle de Neige, a charming, 20-something television weather girl, as "very naive." "She falls in a trap like a poor little lamb and she gets eaten by wolves. "The thing is, she doesn't have a dad, so she lacks affection, and sometimes that lack of affection can drive you to make mistakes. "I'd say I'm stronger than that," says 29 year-old Sagnier, who is perhaps best-known for her provocative portrayal of a highly-sexualized teenager opposite Charlotte Rampling in Francois Ozon's 2003 drama, "Swimming Pool." Sagnier who is often compared with screen sirens like Brigitte Bardot and Catherine Deneuve, drew international acclaim for a series of films in 2002 and 2003, but has recently has been taking smaller roles. Many of the qualities that attracted Sagnier to Chabrol are similar to those that draw her on-screen alter-ego Gabrielle to writer Charles Saint-Denis (Francois Berleand) -- Charles' knowledge of life, literature and his ability to treat her like a little girl, not as an equal. Sagnier says of working with Chabrol: "It was like opening a cinema book, because when you work with him he talks to you about Hitchcock, he talks to you about Kubrick. "He met everyone, so he's full of anecdotes, so you want to know more." Chabrol began his career in 1956, earning his stripes alongside fellow New Wave directors Jean-Luc Godard and Francois Truffaut. He became famous in the late 1960s for suspense thrillers such as "La Femme Infidele" (1969) and "Le Boucher" (1971). He has continued working prolifically in film and television ever since. Chabrol co-wrote the screenplay for the heartbreak drama, in which Sagnier character is consistently disappointed in love and let down by the men around her, with his step-daughter, Cecile Maistre, who also served as assistant director on the film. At the end of "The Girl Cut In Two," Sagnier appears on stage as a magician's assistant, smiling in the spotlight as she hears applause rise from the audience, the attention perhaps curing her depression over lovers lost. She lies in a box, appearing to be cut in half, the trick functioning as an almost literal embodiment of the film's title -- but clearly there's more to it than meets the eye. "She cuts into two men first of all, and she's also cut in two different sides of her personality," said Sagnier. "She has a part of shade and a part of lightness." Sagnier's fate since her collaboration with Chabrol has, thankfully, been a decidedly rosier affair: Since finishing "The Girl Cut in Two," she has starred in Jean-Francois Richet's, "Public Enemy No. 1," which received more nominations than any other film at the 2009 Cesar Awards, France's equivalent of the Oscars. The indefatigable Chabrol has recently wrapped up yet another film: "Bellamy" starring Gerard Depardieu. "The Girl Cut In Two" is released in the UK on 22 May 2009 .

LONDON, England (CNN) -- When a woman dates a much older man, bystanders often speculate that her motives are of the most superficial kind. Yet in "The Girl Cut in Two," veteran French filmmaker Claude Chabrol tells the story of a young woman for whom precisely the opposite holds true.

The film stars French actress Ludivine Sagnier as a young woman who rebuffs the amorous advances of a flashy, wealthy man her own age in favor of a sordid affair with a fickle, sixty-year-old father figure. Fittingly, Sagnier's own desire to take on the role was itself inspired by the allure of a much older man: Chabrol himself.

"The idea of working with Claude Chabrol was the main attraction at the beginning," she told CNN. "He is a great French director, one of the pioneers of the French New Wave."

"The man has so much experience. I felt as though I were a journalist, forever asking questions," Sagnier continued. "He's very old ... he's been through so many things. This was his sixty-sixth film, or something to that effect."

Sagnier describes her character, Gabrielle de Neige -- a charming television weather girl in her twenties -- as "very naïve."

"She falls into a trap like a poor little lamb, only to be devoured by wolves," she explained. "The thing is, she has no father, so she is starved of affection, and sometimes that absence of affection can drive you to make mistakes."

"I'd like to think I'm stronger than that," says the 29-year-old Sagnier, who is perhaps best known for her provocative portrayal of a highly sexualized teenager opposite Charlotte Rampling in François Ozon's 2003 drama "Swimming Pool."

Sagnier -- frequently compared to screen sirens such as Brigitte Bardot and Catherine Deneuve -- earned international acclaim for a string of films in 2002 and 2003, but has more recently gravitated toward smaller roles.

Many of the qualities that drew Sagnier to Chabrol mirror those that draw her on-screen counterpart, Gabrielle, to the writer Charles Saint-Denis (François Berléand): his worldly knowledge of life and literature, and his tendency to treat her like a little girl rather than an equal.

Of working with Chabrol, Sagnier reflects: "It was like opening a book on cinema, because when you work with him, he talks to you about Hitchcock, he talks to you about Kubrick. He has met everyone, so he is full of anecdotes, and it leaves you wanting to know more."

Chabrol launched his career in 1956, earning his stripes alongside fellow New Wave directors Jean-Luc Godard and François Truffaut. He rose to prominence in the late 1960s with suspense thrillers such as "La Femme Infidèle" (1969) and "Le Boucher" (1971), and has continued to work prolifically in film and television ever since.

Chabrol co-wrote the screenplay for this tale of heartbreak -- in which Sagnier's character is perpetually disappointed in love and let down by the men around her -- with his stepdaughter, Cécile Maistre, who also served as the film's assistant director.

At the close of "The Girl Cut in Two," Sagnier appears on stage as a magician's assistant, smiling in the spotlight as applause swells from the audience -- the attention perhaps soothing her heartache over lovers lost. She lies within a box, seemingly cut in half, the illusion serving as an almost literal embodiment of the film's title -- though there is clearly more to it than meets the eye.

"First of all, she cuts into two men, and she is also divided between two sides of her personality," said Sagnier. "There is a part of her in shadow and a part of her in light."

Sagnier's own fortunes since her collaboration with Chabrol have, thankfully, proven a decidedly rosier affair. Since completing "The Girl Cut in Two," she has starred in Jean-François Richet's "Public Enemy No. 1," which garnered more nominations than any other film at the 2009 César Awards, France's equivalent of the Oscars.

The indefatigable Chabrol, meanwhile, has recently wrapped yet another film: "Bellamy," starring Gérard Depardieu.

"The Girl Cut in Two" is released in the UK on 22 May 2009.

"Claude had this remarkable calm on set," she recalled. "He knew exactly what he wanted, but he gave you room to breathe as an actor. There was no anxiety, just this quiet confidence. You felt you were in the hands of someone who had seen everything cinema could offer."

For Sagnier, who first gained international attention in François Ozon's "Swimming Pool," the part offered a chance to work within the tradition of French auteur cinema she had long admired.

"To work with Chabrol is to become part of history," she said. "He filmed France's soul—its beauty and its cruelty. I feel privileged to have been directed by him."

# The Muse and the Master: Ludivine Sagnier and Claude Chabrol's "The Girl Cut in Two"

## A Collaboration Between New Wave Royalty and a New Generation

There's a particular kind of magic that happens when a director in the twilight of a legendary career finds a performer capable of embodying his most enduring obsessions. In *The Girl Cut in Two* (*La Fille coupée en deux*, 2007), Claude Chabrol discovered that alchemy in Ludivine Sagnier, crafting a film that both looks back at his decades-long fascination with bourgeois hypocrisy and forward toward a fresh cinematic energy.

## The Story: A Modern Love Triangle Turned Dangerous

The film follows Gabrielle Deneige, a bright and ambitious young television weather presenter in Lyon whose life becomes ensnared between two very different men. On one side stands Charles Saint-Denis (François Berléand), a celebrated, married novelist decades her senior—cultured, seductive, and ultimately manipulative. On the other is Paul Gaudens (Benoît Magimel), a volatile heir to a pharmaceutical fortune, whose passionate pursuit curdles into possessive obsession.

Loosely inspired by the real-life 1906 murder of architect Stanford White by Harry Kendall Thaw over the affections of showgirl Evelyn Nesbit, Chabrol transplants the scandal to contemporary France. What emerges is a study of how a woman becomes the terrain upon which two men wage a battle of ego, class, and desire—the "girl cut in two" of the title referring both literally and metaphorically to Gabrielle's fate.

## Sagnier's Gabrielle: Innocence and Complicity

For Sagnier, then in her late twenties and already known internationally for her provocative turn in François Ozon's *Swimming Pool* (2003), Gabrielle offered a role of remarkable delicacy. The character walks a razor's edge—neither pure victim nor calculating opportunist, but a young woman genuinely caught between competing forms of exploitation.

Sagnier brings a luminous ambiguity to the part. Her Gabrielle is intelligent yet naïve, sensual yet vulnerable, and the actress refuses to let the audience settle comfortably into judgment. It's a performance built on subtle gradations rather than dramatic outbursts, requiring the kind of restraint that Chabrol famously prized in his leading women. She joins a distinguished lineage of Chabrol muses—from Stéphane Audran to Isabelle Huppert—who understood that his cinema thrives in the space between what is said and what is concealed.

## Chabrol: The Last of the New Wave

By the time he made *The Girl Cut in Two*, Claude Chabrol was one of the last surviving pillars of the French New Wave. His 1958 debut *Le Beau Serge* is often cited as one of the movement's founding films, and across a career spanning more than fifty features, he earned comparisons to Alfred Hitchcock for his cool, ironic dissections of the murderous impulses lurking beneath respectable surfaces.

Films like *Les Biches* (1968), *La Femme infidèle* (1969), and *Le Boucher* (1970) established his signature: the meticulous, almost surgical examination of the French bourgeoisie, whose polished manners so often masked appetite, cruelty, and violence. Where his New Wave contemporaries Godard and Truffaut pursued formal revolution, Chabrol preferred a classical elegance, letting his critique emerge through irony rather than provocation.

*The Girl Cut in Two* fits comfortably within this tradition. The film is less interested in the mechanics of its melodrama than in the corrupt social world that produces it—the smug literary establishment, the decadent aristocracy, the media culture that treats a young woman as spectacle. Chabrol observes it all with his characteristic detachment, neither condemning nor excusing, simply exposing.

## A Meeting of Sensibilities

What makes the collaboration compelling is the generational dialogue it stages. Chabrol, then in his late seventies, brings the accumulated wisdom of a master who has spent a lifetime watching how power operates in intimate relationships. Sagnier, representing a new wave of French acting talent unafraid of complex, sexually frank material, gives that vision a contemporary immediacy.

The result is a film that feels simultaneously timeless and current—a late-career work that demonstrates Chabrol had lost none of his precision or his mordant wit. He would make only a couple more films before his death in 2010, lending *The Girl Cut in Two* additional resonance as one of the final statements from a filmmaker who spent half a century watching civilized people behave abominably.

## Legacy

Neither Chabrol's most celebrated work nor a minor footnote, *The Girl Cut in Two* stands as an elegant capstone collaboration—proof that the master's fascinations remained vital, and that in Sagnier he found a performer worthy of carrying them. For audiences discovering Chabrol through this film, it serves as an ideal gateway to a body of work that quietly, insistently insisted on the darkness at the heart of polite society.

# The Enigmatic Muse: Ludivine Sagnier on Chabrol's Legacy and the Art of French Cinema

*An in-depth conversation with one of France's most compelling actresses about her latest project, the shadows of the past, and the enduring magic of cinema's boldest movement*

---

There is a particular quality to the way Ludivine Sagnier occupies a room—an alertness, a coiled intelligence behind those luminous eyes that have graced French cinema for over two decades. When we meet in a sunlit café in Paris's 6th arrondissement, she orders an espresso and settles into her chair with the unhurried grace of someone who has learned that the best performances, on screen and off, require patience.

"People always want to talk about beginnings," she tells me, a slight smile playing at her lips. "But I find myself increasingly interested in what things *mean*—the weight beneath the surface."

That preoccupation with hidden meaning proves fitting, given our subject: her latest film and its deliberately ambiguous title, which she describes as "a doorway into everything the story refuses to say aloud."

## The Weight of a Title

Sagnier leans forward when I ask about the film's name, clearly having anticipated the question.

"A title is never innocent," she says. "The best filmmakers understand this. A title is a promise and a trap at the same time. It tells you where to look while distracting you from what you should actually be seeing."

She speaks of the way the title functions on multiple registers—as literal description, as metaphor, and finally as a kind of moral indictment of the characters who populate the narrative. "On the surface, it names a place, an object. But by the final act, you realize it has been describing the *interior* condition of every person on screen. The title is a mirror. When the lights come up, you understand it was pointing at the audience all along."

This layered approach to symbolism, she notes, connects her contemporary work to a specific tradition in French filmmaking—one embodied by the director who has shaped her understanding of the craft more than any other: Claude Chabrol.

## The Shadow of Chabrol

Though Sagnier's latest film is not directed by Chabrol—who passed away in 2010—his influence hovers over our entire conversation like a benevolent ghost. She worked with the legendary director in *The Girl Cut in Two* (2007), an experience she describes as formative.

"Chabrol taught me that evil wears a very ordinary face," she says. "He was fascinated by the bourgeoisie—by the beautiful houses and the good manners and the terrible things happening just beneath the tablecloth. He would smile while he showed you the rot. That was his genius."

For those unfamiliar with his towering contribution to cinema, Claude Chabrol was one of the founding fathers of the French New Wave, or *Nouvelle Vague*. Born in 1930, he began his career, like many of his peers, as a critic for the influential film magazine *Cahiers du Cinéma*. In 1958, his debut feature *Le Beau Serge* is often credited as one of the first films of the movement—a low-budget, location-shot drama that broke definitively from the polished studio productions of the French cinematic establishment.

"He was there at the very beginning," Sagnier reminds me. "Before it even had a name."

## Understanding the New Wave

The French New Wave, which flourished from the late 1950s through the 1960s, represented nothing less than a revolution in how films could be made and what they could be about. Alongside Chabrol stood a constellation of young iconoclasts: François Truffaut, Jean-Luc Godard, Éric Rohmer, and Jacques Rivette, among others. United in their rejection of what Truffaut famously derided as the "Tradition of Quality"—the stately, literary French cinema of the postwar era—these filmmakers championed a more personal, spontaneous, and formally adventurous approach.

They shot on location with lightweight cameras. They embraced natural lighting, improvised dialogue, and jarring editing techniques like the jump cut. Above all, they advocated for the *politique des auteurs*—the "auteur theory"—which held that the director was the true author of a film, imprinting it with a personal vision as distinctive as a novelist's prose.

"The New Wave gave permission," Sagnier explains. "Permission to be imperfect, to be human, to point the camera at real life and trust that it was enough. That freedom is still what I chase in every role."

Chabrol, for his part, carved a particular niche within the movement. While Godard grew increasingly experimental and political, Chabrol found his voice in the psychological thriller, earning comparisons to Alfred Hitchcock—a filmmaker he revered and about whom he co-wrote an influential critical study. Across films like *Les Biches* (1968), *La Femme infidèle* (1969), and *Le Boucher* (1970), Chabrol dissected the hypocrisies of French middle-class life with a cold, clinical precision that was nonetheless suffused with dark humor.

## A Continuing Conversation

When I ask how Chabrol's lessons manifest in her new film, Sagnier grows thoughtful.

"My character in this film would have fascinated him," she says. "She is a woman who has constructed an entire identity around a lie—not to deceive others, but to survive her own truth. Chabrol always understood that the most dangerous secrets are the ones we keep from ourselves."

She describes the process of building the role as an act of "controlled excavation," peeling back layers of pretense over the course of the narrative until the audience—and the character herself—confronts the emptiness at the center. It is a structure that echoes the very symbolism of the title we discussed earlier: the mirror that reflects not what we wish to see, but what we are.

"That is the through-line from Chabrol to now," she says. "The refusal to let the audience off easily. The insistence that beauty and horror can share the same frame."

## The Actress at This Moment

At this stage in her career, Sagnier moves fluidly between French and international productions, between cinema and prestige television—she earned wide acclaim for her role in *The New Pope* opposite Jude Law and John Malkovich. Yet she remains rooted in the traditions that formed her.

"I am a product of French cinema," she says without apology. "Of its arguments, its excesses, its refusal to be comfortable. When I read a script now, I ask myself: what would Chabrol have seen here? Where is the rot beneath the tablecloth?"

As our conversation winds down, I return one final time to the question of the title—that layered, deceptive doorway into the film's meaning.

"By the end," she says, gathering her coat, "you understand that the title was never really about the story at all. It was about *you*—the person watching in the dark, recognizing something you didn't want to admit. That is what great cinema does. That is what Chabrol did. And that," she adds with a final, enigmatic smile, "is what I still hope to do, every single time."

She rises, thanks me warmly, and steps out into the Parisian afternoon—leaving behind, like the films she so admires, the sense of a mystery only partially solved.
